concept.name: Rate Limiting Algorithms & Token Buckets
concept.tagline: Protecting APIs from abuse, resource exhaustion, and cascading thundering herds.

spark.summary: Rate limiting controls the consumption rate of system resources by restricting the number of API calls or operations a client can make within a specified window. Proper rate limiting prevents denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, isolates noisy tenants in multi-tenant architectures, smooths burst traffic, and enforces commercial usage quotas.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use the Token Bucket algorithm for burst-tolerant API gateways. Execute atomic Redis Lua scripts to prevent distributed race conditions without multi-node locks.

concept.whyItMatters: Without rate limiting, a single rogue script, buggy mobile app retry loop, or malicious DDoS flood will exhaust database connection pools, spike CPU to 100%, and take down the entire platform for all users.
keyPoints: Token Bucket: Tokens refill at a constant rate $r$ up to capacity $b$. Requests consume tokens. Handles bursts gracefully.
Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue processed at a steady rate. Smooths out traffic into a constant egress stream.
Fixed Window: Counts requests per fixed minute/hour window. Vulnerable to 2x burst spikes at window boundaries.
Sliding Window Log: Tracks exact timestamps in a sorted set (ZSET). Accurate but memory intensive.
Atomic Execution: Distributed counters must use Redis Lua scripts or single-threaded atomic operations to prevent concurrency race conditions.
whenToUse: Public REST/GraphQL API Gateways (Kong, Envoy, AWS API Gateway) to protect backend microservices.
Preventing brute-force credential stuffing attacks on authentication endpoints.
Enforcing tiered subscription billing and third-party SaaS rate caps.
whenNotToUse: Internal, low-latency inter-process communication within a trusted private cluster where backpressure should be managed via reactive streams.

examples.title: Thwarting a Thundering Herd Login Spike
examples.scenario: A flash sale notification causes 100,000 users to hit /api/login at the same second. A Token Bucket rate limiter caps each IP to 5 req/sec with a burst of 10.
examples.outcome: Rogue bots receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests; genuine users log in smoothly without auth database overload.

tradeOffs.pro: Token Bucket requires only 10 bytes per user (2 bytes tokens + 8 bytes timestamp).
tradeOffs.con: Sliding Window Log tracks every request timestamp, consuming 20–50 bytes per request and requiring periodic compaction.

failureModes.name: Distributed Redis Counter Race Condition
failureModes.description: Separate GET and SET operations in Redis allow concurrent requests to read the same remaining token count, causing double-spending and quota bypass.
failureModes.mitigation: Execute counter decrements inside an atomic Redis Lua script.

commonMistakes: Hard-failing during rate limiter cluster downtime instead of configuring a fail-open policy.
Rate limiting solely on IP address, which penalizes corporate networks or mobile carriers where thousands of users share a single NAT gateway IP.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 Operational Architecture of Distributed Rate Limiting

### 1. Algorithm Comparison Matrix

| Algorithm | Burst Handling | Memory Overhead | Time Complexity | Best Suited For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Token Bucket** | Excellent (burst up to capacity $b$) | Minimal ($O(1)$ per client: ~10 bytes) | $O(1)$ | General-purpose API gateways, AWS/Stripe-style APIs |
| **Leaky Bucket** | None (forces smooth, constant outflow) | Minimal ($O(\text{queue size})$) | $O(1)$ | Egress message queues, disk write throttling |
| **Fixed Window** | Poor (up to 2x burst at boundary) | Minimal ($O(1)$) | $O(1)$ | Simple cron quotas, non-critical hourly caps |
| **Sliding Window Log** | Perfect accuracy | High ($O(N)$ requests in window) | $O(\log N)$ | Low-volume, mission-critical financial transactions |
| **Sliding Window Counter** | High accuracy (weighted average) | Minimal ($O(1)$ per window) | $O(1)$ | High-scale APIs (Cloudflare rate limiting) |

---

### 2. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimation

- **Scale:** Assume an API serves **10,000,000 Daily Active Users (DAU)**.
- **Throughput:** Average $\sim 50,000$ QPS; peak $\sim 100,000$ QPS.
- **Memory Footprint:** 
  $$\text{Per-User Memory} = 2\text{ bytes (token count)} + 8\text{ bytes (last-updated timestamp)} = 10\text{ bytes}$$
  $$\text{Total Memory} = 10\text{ bytes} \times 10,000,000\text{ users} = 100\text{ MB}$$
  $100\text{ MB}$ easily fits in the RAM of a single Redis instance, though sharded across a cluster for high availability.

---

### 3. Production Atomic Redis Lua Script

```lua
-- Redis Lua Script for Atomic Token Bucket Rate Limiting
local key = KEYS[1]
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local refill_rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4] or 1)

local data = redis.call("HMGET", key, "tokens", "last_updated")
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local last_updated = tonumber(data[2])

if tokens == null then
    tokens = capacity
    last_updated = now
else
    local elapsed = math.max(0, now - last_updated)
    tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refill_rate)
    last_updated = now
end

if tokens >= requested then
    tokens = tokens - requested
    redis.call("HMSET", key, "tokens", tokens, "last_updated", last_updated)
    redis.call("EXPIRE", key, math.ceil(capacity / refill_rate) * 2)
    return 1 -- Allowed
else
    redis.call("HMSET", key, "tokens", tokens, "last_updated", last_updated)
    return 0 -- Denied (HTTP 429)
end
```

questions.title: Atomic Counter Rate Limiting Under Concurrency
questions.prompt: Why are standard Redis GET and SET operations unsafe for implementing API rate limiting across multi-threaded gateway nodes?

options.text: Redis GET and SET require disk I/O flushes that stall execution.
options.explanation: Redis is in-memory and does not flush disk on standard GET/SET.

options.text: Concurrent GET and SET calls create a race condition where multiple requests read identical counter values before incrementing, over-admitting client traffic.
options.explanation: Correct! Non-atomic read-modify-write operations allow clients to bypass rate limits.

rubric.excellent: Identifies race conditions in read-modify-write and suggests Redis Lua scripts or atomic INCR.
rubric.gap: Suggests database transactions for rate counters.

questions.sampleSolution: Non-atomic GET/SET creates race conditions across distributed nodes. Use Redis atomic INCR or Lua scripts.
questions.explanation: Atomic operations prevent concurrent worker threads from reading stale counter values.

interviewProblems.title: Global Multi-Region API Rate Limiter
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are building an API Gateway for a global cloud provider serving 500,000 requests/sec across 3 geographical regions (US, EU, AP). How do you enforce a strict per-user quota of 1,000 req/min with sub-millisecond overhead?

dimensions.name: Local vs Global Counter Sync
dimensions.description: Decoupling per-region local token buckets from global asynchronous reconciliation.

dimensions.name: Atomic Edge Execution
dimensions.description: Using Redis Lua scripts at edge PoPs.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy local Redis token buckets at each edge region using atomic Lua scripts. Synchronize token usage asynchronously to a global coordinator in batches to avoid cross-region latency on every request.
commonPitfalls: Making synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request.
